node.label: Raewyn Connell
node.date_label: Gender and Power (1987) · Masculinities (1995; second edition 2005) · Southern Theory (2007)
node.description: In Masculinities (1995), the sociologist Raewyn Connell argues that masculinities are plural, socially made and organized through unequal relations of power. Hegemonic masculinity names the dominant pattern within this hierarchy of masculinities, understood as a historically changing relation of power rather than a fixed trait of individual men. Joy Parr drew on Connell’s studies of social practice in The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), and John Tosh later acknowledged Gender and Power (1987) as a theoretical resource for Manful Assertions (1991). The framework also drew serious criticism. In their 2005 reconsideration, Connell and James W. Messerschmidt accepted the critique of trait models and rigid typologies, recognized that subordinated masculinities can influence dominant forms, and called for a more complex model of gender hierarchy that emphasizes the agency of women. Tosh subsequently defended contextual case studies against the emphasis on broad historical narratives in Connell’s “The Big Picture” (1993). Southern Theory (2007) extended Connell’s criticism of metropolitan universals to the global production of social knowledge.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Gender and Power (1987); Masculinities (1995; second edition 2005); The Men and the Boys (2000); Gender (2002); “Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept” (2005), with James W. Messerschmidt; Southern Theory (2007); Gender: In World Perspective (2009, revised second edition); “Transsexual Women and Feminist Thought” (2012); The Good University (2019).
node.scope_note: The 2005 joint article was read only in its published abstract; selected passages of the 2011 interview published in 2013, Parr’s introduction pp. 8–9, and Tosh’s reflection and the editors’ introduction in the open-access 2024 volume were read. Masculinities and Southern Theory were not read in full. The 2012 Signs article was read only as a publisher abstract; other selected books are represented through metadata, publisher descriptions and explicitly attributed retrospective discussion. Demetriou’s original article, Bourdieu’s book and Connell’s 1993 essay remain unread.

people_update.label: Raewyn Connell
people_update.identity_note: Connell describes herself as a transsexual woman; most of her earlier work was published as R. W. Connell.

proposed_edges.relationship: The editors’ introduction to Men and Masculinities in Modern Britain (2024) traces Connell’s theory of hegemony to a broader turn to Gramscian models in the social sciences and New Left politics of the 1970s and 1980s.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read Houlbrook, Jones and Mechen’s introduction to Men and Masculinities in Modern Britain (publisher release 2024), printed p. 37 n. 30 (PDF page 46), in the publisher’s open-access edition deposited at UCL: https://discovery.ucl.ac.uk/id/eprint/10190042/1/9781526174703_fullhl.pdf . The editors situate Connell’s theory within a wider Gramscian turn. This is their retrospective attribution, not a debt stated by Connell and not a reading of the 2005 joint article. Retain the mediated/thin qualification. Source rc_w_mup_intro_2024 already exists in the supplied input and is already cited by this edge; no duplicate source is needed.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2011 interview published in 2013, Connell recalls that her first book of social theory, Which Way Is Up?, set out to move Australian social theory away from Talcott Parsons and toward Freud and Sartre, feminism, education and equality.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on rc_w_interview2013; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. Connell's own interview (permitted, SciELO) supports a narrower claim of engagement with Freud. The interview gives no year for Which Way Is Up? (it is usually dated 1983; the coordinator should confirm it before adding a year). Weak: flag as thin, or hold if the coordinator wants a stated debt. Phrase seen: “Which Way is Up? foi uma tentativa de trazer a teoria social da Austrália para o mundo real, parar de falar de Talcott Parsons e companhia, e começar a falar de Freud e Sartre”

proposed_edges.relationship: In Southern Theory (2007), as Connell recounts in her 2011 interview published in 2013, she follows a critique of Eurocentrism in social thought with criticisms of Bourdieu, Giddens and other modern metropolitan theorists.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on rc_w_interview2013; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. Connell's interview supports a different, permitted claim: criticism of Bourdieu in Southern Theory (2007). Phrase seen: “Começo com uma espécie de crítica ao eurocentrismo no pensamento social. Critico isso - e prossigo com críticas a Bourdieu, a Giddens e a algumas teorias modernas”

proposed_edges.relationship: In The Gender of Breadwinners (1990), Parr aligns her questions about fixed categories of gender and class with those raised in Connell’s studies of social practice, gender and power, and adopts Connell’s suggestion that such meanings are multiple and mutable.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Fresh selected primary reading: Parr, introduction pp.8–9, especially printed p.9 (PDF page 23), paragraph beginning These two ruminations. Parr names Connell alongside Poovey, Scott and Riley, and explicitly invokes meanings as “multiple and mutable”. Does not establish exclusive derivation, agreement on every issue, or a reading of the complete book. Checked against the existing Scott→Parr edge_1683: same passage, different named resource; no Connell→Parr edge exists. Publisher preview: https://api.pageplace.de/preview/DT0400.9781442681347_A35143482/preview-9781442681347_A35143482.pdf .

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Masculinities and history for the present” (2024), Tosh acknowledges Gender and Power (1987) as a theoretical resource for the volume Manful Assertions (1991), which he edited with Michael Roper.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tosh printed p.178, paragraph beginning The history of masculinities, and n.2 on p.185: “theoretical debts” to Segal and Connell; note identifies Gender and Power (1987). Fresh primary retrospective testimony by Tosh, not a fresh reading of the 1991 volume. Shared editorial credit with Roper retained; no separate Roper endpoint is created. Publisher release year is 2024 although deposited PDF imprint says 2023.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Masculinities and history for the present” (2024), Tosh qualifies Connell’s call in “The Big Picture” (1993) for a long history of masculinities, defending contextual case studies as a way to preserve subjectivity and illuminate present problems.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Tosh printed pp.184–185, paragraphs beginning Shortly after Manful Assertions and There are several reasons, through the conclusion; nn.26–28 on p.186 identify Connell’s 1993 essay and The Men and the Boys (2000). The concern is that extended linear history can privilege “power and precept” over interiority. A qualified methodological disagreement, not repudiation of hegemonic masculinity or of the theoretical debt on p.178. Connell’s 1993 essay was not independently read. Distinct claim and direction from rc_w_05.

proposed_edges.relationship: Masculinities (1995), developed and reconsidered with Messerschmidt in “Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept” (2005), supplies gender history with an account of plural, unequal and historically changing masculinities.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Re-based at Claude verification (2026-11-01) on rc_w_interview2013; the essay or article itself was not read on a permitted route, so no page locators from it are used. It is supported by the Crossref/SAGE abstract, the Wiley description ('not one masculinity, but many different masculinities, each associated with different positions of power') and the open-access MUP volume (editors' introduction: 'the intellectual indebtedness of foundational histories of masculinity ... to ... Raewyn Connell'; Tosh p. 178). Phrase seen: “what has been confirmed from early formulations (the idea of multiple masculinities, the concept of hegemony, and the emphasis on change)”

proposed_edges.relationship: In Southern Theory (2007), as Connell explains in her 2011 interview published in 2013, she challenges Eurocentric social theory and argues for treating intellectual work from the global South as theory rather than merely material for metropolitan analysis.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Primary interview, answer beginning Comecei a trabalhar na teoria sulista and continuing through Essa é a história do Southern Theory (SciELO HTML paragraphs at lines165–168), plus the earlier answer about theory dominated by the North. Connell describes her critique and proposed globally democratic social science. Book year confirmed by the interview’s reference list. Southern Theory itself remains unread; claim is explicitly based on her retrospective account. The post endpoint concerns Eurocentric universals and imperial knowledge, so this is an adjacent sociological contribution to that critique, not membership in a uniform school. No community knowledge is reproduced.

proposed_edges.relationship: In their introduction to Nine Centuries of Man (2017), Lynn Abrams and Elizabeth Ewan acknowledge Connell’s Masculinities (1995) as influential in framing their interpretations of relations among men, while emphasizing the contestability of hegemonic masculinity.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the introduction’s discussion on printed pp. 2–3 and its identifying note in the licensed publisher preview. The statement is jointly authored by Abrams and Ewan and explicitly acknowledges influence on their interpretations. This supports a bounded theoretical debt by Abrams, rather than exclusive derivation of the collection’s approach. Ewan is not an eligible endpoint in the supplied lists.
proposed_edges.map_label: Framework for interpreting relations among men

row.context: A sociologist whose account of plural and unequal masculinities became a resource for historians of gender; her later reformulation emphasizes historical change, embodiment and the agency of women.
row.works: Masculinities (1995; second edition 2005); “Hegemonic Masculinity: Rethinking the Concept” (2005), with James W. Messerschmidt.

row.context: Challenges Eurocentric social theory and argues for a more globally democratic production of knowledge; contribution recorded through her own retrospective interview.
